title: ICE Wants to Know Everyone Who Bought a Certain Green Beanie From REI in the Last 2 Years
gist: Homeland Security Investigations used '1509' customs summonses — a tool meant for import/export compliance and sendable without judicial oversight — to subpoena REI, airlines, telecoms, and social platforms for customer data tied to 39 defendants from a Minnesota ICE protest, with companies responding in sharply different ways from full compliance (T-Mobile) to outright refusal (Reddit, Google, Meta).

themes.theme: The REI beanie subpoena and its scope

insights.claim: Homeland Security Investigations agents subpoenaed outdoor retailer REI in March, requesting transaction data for all customers in the greater Minneapolis-St. Paul area who bought a specific dark green beanie from the company since 2024.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: A request for two years of purchase records tied to a single product shows how broadly a customs-related subpoena tool is being applied to ordinary retail data, a precedent relevant to any consumer-facing retailer's data-request policies.
insights.quote: requesting the transaction information for “all persons” in the greater Minneapolis–St. Paul area who had purchased a specific type of dark green beanie from the company since 2024
insights.locator: New court filings allege that Homeland Security Investigations agents subpoenaed

insights.claim: REI did not respond to questions about whether it complied with the beanie-purchaser subpoena or how many customers might be affected.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: REI's silence leaves open whether ordinary customers' purchase histories were actually handed over, an unresolved reputational and privacy-policy question for the retailer.
insights.locator: REI did not respond to questions about whether it had complied

insights.claim: The REI subpoena was one of 92 sent by HSI as part of its investigation, with other recipients including social media companies, airlines, telecom providers, a car rental company, and a state employment agency.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: The scale (92 subpoenas across many industries) indicates a systematic, multi-sector data-collection operation rather than an isolated request, relevant to any company holding consumer transaction, travel, or communications data.
insights.quote: The subpoena to REI was one of 92 sent as part of HSI’s investigation into the defendants
insights.locator: The subpoena to REI was one of 92 sent

insights.claim: At least one subpoena sent to an unnamed airline requested not only a defendant's past flight history but also asked the airline to provide a 'lookout notification' about that defendant's future travel.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: A forward-looking travel 'lookout' request goes beyond historical record retrieval into ongoing surveillance, raising the compliance stakes for airlines handling similar government requests.
insights.quote: asked not only for information about a defendant’s past flights, but also requested that the airline give HSI a “lookout notification” about the defendant’s travel in the future
insights.locator: At least one subpoena sent to an unnamed airline

insights.claim: The subpoenas sent by HSI agents are known as 1509 customs summonses, a legal tool intended for requesting information related to imports and exports, and one that can be issued without judicial or jury oversight.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: The lack of judicial oversight for a tool now being used to identify protesters and journalists is the core legal vulnerability that could invite litigation or legislative reform.
insights.quote: which can be sent without the oversight of a judge or a jury
insights.locator: The subpoenas sent by HSI agents are also known as 1509

insights.claim: Senator Ron Wyden argues that customs summonses are legally limited to requests directly related to customs-law compliance, and that using the tool to search two years of REI's customer data for a political prosecution amounts to a fishing expedition beyond its statutory scope.
insights.speaker: Ron Wyden
insights.so_what: A sitting senator publicly challenging the legal basis of the tool raises the odds of congressional scrutiny or a legislative fix, which is the kind of regulatory catalyst worth monitoring for companies that receive these summonses.
insights.quote: Customs summonses only allow DHS to request information directly related to compliance with customs laws, not to conduct unending fishing expeditions into the lives of people critical of Donald Trump.
insights.locator: “Customs summonses only allow DHS to request information

insights.claim: The total number of 1509 summonses issued since the start of the Trump administration, and how many people have had personal information collected as a result, is unknown because recipient companies are typically instructed to keep the requests secret.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: The absence of any public tally means the true scale of this surveillance program is unmeasurable from outside, making individual leaked cases like REI's the only available signal of its scope.
insights.quote: Companies that receive these types of subpoenas are typically asked to keep their existence a secret.
insights.locator: The total number of 1509 summonses that have been sent

insights.claim: According to a letter from Senator Wyden and Representative Pramila Jayapal, large tech companies sometimes ignore DHS's gag requests when not legally required to comply, while companies in more heavily regulated sectors report complying out of fear of regulatory retaliation.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: This suggests regulatory exposure, not just legal obligation, is driving corporate compliance decisions on data requests — a dynamic relevant to how any regulated company (telecom, finance, healthcare) might weigh pushing back on similar demands.
insights.locator: According to a recent letter written by Wyden and Representative Pramila Jayapal

insights.claim: T-Mobile provided the government six months of journalist Georgia Fort's call and text message logs in response to a customs summons, and attorneys for Fort say neither T-Mobile nor the government ever notified her.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: T-Mobile's compliance without customer notification is a concrete case study of how telecom carriers are handling this legal tool, relevant to assessing telecom-sector privacy risk and disclosure practices.
insights.quote: the government had obtained logs detailing six months’ of Fort’s calls and text messages from T-Mobile after the government sent a customs summons to the telecom provider
insights.locator: Attorneys for Georgia Fort, a journalist and one of the defendants

insights.claim: Google refused to comply with a customs summons seeking information about journalist Georgia Fort's YouTube viewers and subscribers, saying it reviews each government request for lawfulness and works to narrow or reject requests it considers too broad.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: Google's refusal establishes a public precedent of resistance that other platforms and future defendants can point to when contesting similarly broad government demands.
insights.locator: the attorneys said that Google refused to comply with a customs summons

insights.claim: Reddit disclosed that it received DHS administrative subpoenas in the second half of 2025 seeking account information for 11 users who had posted content critical of ICE actions, and that DHS withdrew the subpoenas after Reddit objected on First Amendment grounds.
insights.speaker: Ben Lee
insights.so_what: A successful First Amendment-based pushback that led DHS to withdraw its own subpoenas is a legal template other platforms could use against similar requests.
insights.quote: We routinely push back on law enforcement requests and stand up for users who are exercising their First Amendment rights.
insights.locator: Reddit recently announced that during the last half of 2025

insights.claim: Meta pushed back against at least one customs summons, according to internal DHS correspondence obtained by the Electronic Frontier Foundation, though Meta declined to comment on the matter to WIRED.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: A pattern of major tech platforms (Google, Reddit, Meta) resisting these summonses while telecoms and retailers appear more compliant suggests sector-specific differences in legal posture worth tracking for regulatory or reputational risk.
insights.locator: Meta also pushed back against at least one customs summons

insights.claim: EFF senior staff attorney Mario Trujillo, who tracks DHS subpoenas to tech companies, says DHS has repeatedly proven it cannot be trusted to apply the 1509 customs summons law correctly, and that absent new legislation, companies and their customers are left to fend for themselves.
insights.speaker: Mario Trujillo
insights.so_what: Absent congressional action restricting or penalizing misuse of 1509 summonses, exposure to this kind of broad government data request remains an open-ended compliance and legal risk for any company holding consumer data.
insights.quote: I think DHS has proved time and time again that they can’t be trusted as the stewards of applying this law correctly
insights.locator: “I think DHS has proved time and time again

insights.claim: The subpoenas are part of a broader federal lawsuit against 39 people who attended a protest at a church whose pastor also served as an acting ICE field office director, with defendants including both protesters and journalists covering the event, such as former CNN host Don Lemon.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: Naming journalists covering a protest as legal defendants alongside protesters signals a prosecution strategy that could chill press coverage of similar events, a press-freedom and civil-liberties risk factor.
insights.quote: The filings are part of a broader lawsuit by the federal government against 39 people who attended an ICE protest at a church whose pastor also worked as an acting ICE field office director.
insights.locator: The filings are part of a broader lawsuit
